#3805. Over 2 million Xbox players in the UK and US reportedly used the 'New Zealand trick' to play GTA 6 early - that's more than a third of the country's population

We already knew there'd be a frantic clamour for GTA 6 this week, and we also knew plenty of players would be eyeing up Xbox's 'New Zealand trick' to get in on the action early. But it's now being reported that a whopping 2m UK and US players took advantage of the trick - which, for context, equals more than a third of New Zealand's actual population.

Here's a quick bit of background: Rockstar's regional release schedule meant GTA 6 launched at midnight on 19th November everywhere, local time. As such, New Zealand was the first country in the world to see the hugely anticipated game go live, thanks to timezones. And because Xbox players can make purchases on any regional store easily, simply by changing their console's country, understandably impatient sorts opted to become temporary virtual New Zealand residents in their droves (on PlayStation, the process requires a regional account and payment in local currency so is more finicky).

In fact, according to data analytics firm Ampere Analysis, the early demand was such that 1.5m Xbox users in the US and 600,000 UK Xbox players briefly went Kiwi for the occasion of GTA 6's launch. Other countries highlighted by Ampere include Canada, where 200,000 Xbox players took the New Zealand plunge, Brazil (200,000 players), and Mexico (100,000 players).

By contrast, just 100,000 PlayStation players in the US opted to dive in early, reflecting, as Ampere notes, "the ease of being able to switch country in the account settings on Xbox consoles." And here's all that info in graph form:

Amusingly, New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first."

Some hours later and the rest of the world can now finally, officially join in the GTA 6 fun, and it's a game worth playing. Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell called it an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in his five star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#3803. Nvidia's latest graphics card driver appears to be unnecessarily writing to PC SSDs, something that's dumb, annoying and definitely warrants reverting

Ooh, an Nvidia-related story that isn't about their now former CEO allegedly getting amorous with someone. I wonder what it's abou-oh. Oh no. It looks like Nvidia's latest GeForce driver, 621.24, is needlessly writing vast amounts of data to PC SSDs.

As noted by PC Gamer, reports of driver 621.24 writing more than it should to SSDs have popped up across various forums and Reddit.

Some instances of the bug, which doesn't appear to be affecting everyone, have the driver writing up to 30GB every hour. For context, it'd take a bugged driver writing that much thousands of hours to break a gaming SSD with a typical endurance rating in the hundreds of terabytes. However, that doesn't mean this is anything less than a pretty bad bug. As such, reverting to the previous driver, 621.01, is a good idea if you're on 621.24 and suspect it of writing chunks of gigabytes to your SSD.

In order to check if that's going on, open task manager, head to the 'details' tab, right click on the column header, click 'select columns', select 'I/O write bytes' from the menu of check boxes that brings up, then look for 'NVDisplay.Container.exe'. The number next that exe is in bytes, so you'll need to do a bit of maths to work out if it's writing mere MB or globs of GB.

Bizarrely, the affected 621.24 driver still hasn't been pulled by Nvidia as of writing, meaning it can still be downloaded by people who might not be aware of any issues and think 'ooh, haven't checked I'm on the latest driver in a while.' The driver was released on November 12th, so it's not a brand new arrival that the company just haven't had a chance to look into yet.

Here's hoping that it is fixed or replaced ASAP, if it hasn't been by the time you read this. AMD look to have dealt with a similar issue recently, and I'd like to think driver updates across all cards aren't going to be some form of permanent Russian roulette going forwards.

#3802. Ubisoft cuts jobs at major Assassin's Creed and Far Cry studios as its year of layoffs continues

Ubisoft has confirmed more layoffs as part of its previously announced operational "reset", this time affecting 166 employees at its major Montréal and Québec City studios - the teams responsible for game series including Assassin's Creed and Far Cry. It says the cuts are necessary "to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs."

GamesIndustry.biz reports the cuts - believed to equate to around four percent of the studios' total headcount - will impact employees working on projects either recently cancelled or significantly changed.

The publication also understands the cuts, said to primarily impact production and support roles at Ubisoft Montréal and Québec City, include members of Vantage Studios - Ubisoft and Tencent's joint development venture announced last October, which focuses on the publisher's biggest franchises, including Far Cry, Rainbow Six Siege, and Assassin's Creed.

In a statement provided to Eurogamer, Ubisoft confirmed it is, "reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations", adding: "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

"We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues," the statement continued. "We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources."

These latest job cuts are part of a "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" announced by Ubisoft in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

Since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

#3798. GTA 6 players are being abducted by aliens and knocked out by Bigfoot

Grand Theft Auto 6 has only been out for a matter of hours, and players have already tracked down a UFO in the woods and a Bigfoot in the swamps.

The UFO encounter is a random night-time event in Kelly County, on a dirt road near the Starlet Motel safehouse east of Port Gellhorn. You'll need to have finished the game's first chapter, and it's most reliable after 2am in-game.

As word spread late yesterday (18th November), it seems the event will kick off if you find a car at the side of the road with its headlights flickering, its trunk open, and clothes strewn around it. Follow the trail into the trees towards a blue glow, and you'll catch a UFO beaming down on a woman before it drops her and flies off. Head back to her car, as she requests, and the UFO returns for you. You apparently black out and come round three days later, and a bronze trophy called The Truth Is Out There should unlock.

You can seemingly trigger the event as either Jason or Lucia, and it isn't needed for 100 percent completion.

And that's not the only close encounter you can expect, either. YouTuber Lazarbeam bumped into Bigfoot on the afternoon of 18th November, hours before the game launched in the UK, while one Reddit user reported that they weren't quite sure what they'd stumbled on, titling their post "I think I found Bigfoot".

Leonida's version of Bigfoot is actually the Skunk Ape, Florida's own swamp cryptid, and it can be found in the swamplands near Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County as soon as free roam opens up. Listen out for a loud roar, then use Jason's tracking ability to follow it through the swamp. You may find it feeding on a deer carcass, while a second sighting has been reported south of Watson Bay.

Either way, the trail seemingly ends at a strange, human-like tree. Investigate it, and Jason blacks out, triggering a short cutscene in which the creature creeps up on him, as shown in this video. He later wakes near his vehicle, drenched in sweat. Save your ammo, though, as shooting at it won't do you any good.

Cryptids and aliens are, of course, something of a Rockstar tradition by this point. GTA 5's Mount Chiliad mystery kept players hunting for years, and Output Lag has already spotted two NPCs in a GTA 6 bar talking about goings-on there. Nobody has cracked a full Chiliad-style puzzle in the new game yet, but I'm sure that's just a matter of when, not if.

GTA 6 launched today on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, although some have been getting in on the action earlier as a whopping 2m Xbox players in the UK and US took advantage of the trick of changing their console's country. Even New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty. "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first."

#3796. Darkest Dungeon 2's next bit of DLC is a short run, combat focused gauntlet where you must do everything in your power to please the audience

The original Darkest Dungeon may have gotten some new DLC earlier this year, but that doesn't mean that Red Hook Studios are abandoning their sequel. No, in fact the next bit of DLC for Darkest Dungeon 2 was teased only a couple of weeks ago, with a new trailer shared today actually showing off what it's all about.

It's called The Butcher's Asylum, as pleasant a name as any other, and it's a "stand alone gladiatorial arena game mode," that's due for release sometime in 2027. "The long-silent bells of the remote Asylum ring once more - souring the valley below with discordant and unsettling vibrations," the DLC's Steam page describes. "Garish heraldry, hastily stitched by unskilled hands, festoons the hilltop. Deep within the crumbling masonry of the Asylum, frenzied inmates compete in merciless bloodsport with monsters corralled the kingdom over. And to the victors of these debauched contests, the Butcher’s favour: a cure for their madness."

This DLC isn't veering too far away from its roguelite origins, as it is still run-based, just on the shorter side and focusing more on the combat system. On your runs you'll need to prepare for the fights ahead, come across "insane enemy combinations never before possible," and spin a fun wheel which nets you prizes like new battle modifiers, charms and jinxes. There's also a new crowd meter, "a unique feature to the Asylum, can grant powerful effects to your team if you cater to the Crowd's demands. Failing to do so will only earn their scorn which raises the stakes and puts your success in jeopardy!"

The Butcher's Asylum also introduces a new playable character, The Ringmaster. You pick her up by winning bouts in the arena, and then you can recruit her in any game mode. She also serves as the narrator for the DLC, likely because of the passing of the main game's narrator Wayne June; Red Hook made clear earlier this year that they would never use generative AI to recreate June's voice, so I'm glad to see they haven't backstracked here.

Get a premium TV without spending too much

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you want to enjoy your games, TV shows and movies, getting a good-looking screen is half of the battle. OLED TVs are some of the best out there, due to the screen tech offering unmatched contrast and true darkness. Only, there's a catch.

OLED TVs are some of the most expensive out there. That's why a Black Friday deal is helpful: it lets you pick up an expensive set at a greatly reduced cost. These sets are so expensive that discounts of hundreds, even thousands, of dollars are commonplace. To help you find a Black Friday deal on an OLED TV you should own, I've found three deals in three different price brackets: some more affordable models under $799, a handful of mid-rangers under $1,499, and then some premium options for more than that.

One of Samsung's most affordable TVs, this set has been slowly dropping in price for the last few months, and now it's at its lowest-ever price. Multiple size models are reduced, but the 48-incher is the one which sits under the price threshold.

LG has plenty of sets in the sales, and this model is its cheapest OLED worth considering. It's over half off, marking the biggest price discount of any budget OLED set.

A more premium LG offering, this set is discounted more at Walmart than at other retailers. We've never seen the 42-inch model go this cheap before, and other sizes are discounted albeit not as much.

Sitting right on the border between budget and mid-range is Roku, which often makes affordable tech, and that's why you can get a 65-inch OLED for a relatively low price. This is a new low price for the set.

Most retailers are selling this set for $800 off, but Amazon's beaten them by a hair. Sony Bravia sets are usually premium and expensive sets, so a discount on one is worth leaping at.

Another LG TV, and another deal in which Amazon undercuts other retailers, by $50 this time. This is the lowest price LG's OLED has sold for, although it's only a hair below the previous best price.

For a deal on a bigger set, and at a size which some other retailers aren't stocking, this Samsung OLED is nearly half-off. Some other sizes are on offer too, but several are selling out.

This well-received TV set from 2026 is quite new to be getting a big discount, albeit a smaller saving than some alternatives. It's not as big as some other discounted TVs, but you're paying for a brand-new set.

A nice four-figure discount on this premium Sony Bravia set, which also brings it to its lowest-ever price. It uses Quantum Dot OLED, which offers even more vivid color than OLED usually does.

If you're looking for a nice new gaming TV, you don't need OLED, of course. Your console or docked handheld will work just as well if you don't stretch for the premium tech.

OLED is only to be seriously considered if you're putting some money towards a fancy home theater set-up, and want a great set to be part of that. OLED offers true blacks as the LEDs turn totally off, unlike on an LCD-based set, and the tech also offers more vivid colors, better contrast and wider viewing angles.

Some LCD technologies offer similar benefits at a lower price. Mini LED and QLED both use smaller backlights to offer great contrast in different ways, and some brands have their own technology to solve the LED shortcomings.

Screen tech isn't the only consideration too. If you're buying a set for gaming, you'll need to look into the number of ports and space behind the set, while screen size, operating system and mounting are all things to decide on before you buy a set.

"Another fun statistic for you! #WoWForever has more people playing weekly than we've seen in World of Warcraft in 15 years!" executive producer and World of Warcraft vice president Holly Longdale posted. "Thank you all for joining us in Azeroth. We're doing this together, for Forever!"

#3791. "Everyone agrees it's more fun this way": Toby Fox won't tell his team how Deltarune ends until they've built enough of it

"Just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading…"

Toby Fox is a purposefully mysterious person. It was probably a wise choice on his part, obfuscating his current appearance with everyone's favourite annoying dog, essentially never speaking aloud in livestreams and instead using a text-to-speech bot, and posting only when there's notable enough Deltarune updates of if it would be very funny. But as it turns out, that sense of mystery extends to the team that's making Deltarune too, as Fox won't tell his devs how the game ends until they've built enough of it.

Earlier this week, the fall edition of the Deltarune newsletter went out, offering a brief update on the game's next and sixth chapter. That one's apparently now a "structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end," but that doesn't mean it's quite ready for release, as "some important scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation." I'd expect a 2027 release for this chapter, which is going to be a shorter one too.

But in typical tricky Tony fashion, there's an update for chapter seven where he makes it sound like no one but him knows how the whole game is going to end. "Well, we've only just started…," he explains of the progress. "I read out the events and dialogue of Chapter 7 to the team. However, just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading… I told my team they need to complete more of the game before I tell them what happens. Everyone agrees it's more fun this way."

I'm glad they all think it's fun, the wait for me personally certainly ain't. I do wonder if this speaks to a certain anxiety over how the game will shape up. Following the release of chapter five I was subjected to all manner of theories about what's to come by my partner gorging on YouTube videos from folks who mostly just seem quite excited about it all, even if a lot of them sound wrong. So I imagine there must be a little bit of weight to all of those varying expectations.

Fox did note in the newsletter that "unlike every other Chapter, I actually feel like I know what I'm doing this time, so I have a lot of confidence...!" so perhaps I'm speaking a load of hogwash! That said, I'm furious that a character called Apple Girlington didn't make it into chapter five, so you can expect to hear from my lawyers, Mr. Fox.

CyberLeek, the persona of a hacker group that was responsible for leaking GTA 6 gameplay before the game launched, has reappeared today, claiming to have released a development build of the final version of the game on its site. This new leak appears to be making good on a threat posted back in October, where the group stated its intent to release a full, playable build of the game.

Various social media accounts have visited the site and noted the size of the download offered by CyberLeek is, indeed 209GB. Eurogamer has seen the site and can confirm this is what the group has claimed, however I have been unable to verify the existence of any actual files. On the site, CyberLeek claims this build is from November 2026 - meaning it is very close to (if not the actual) release build. The 'executable file appears to be missing from the build, however, meaning you cannot actually - yet - get it up and running. CyberLeek is threatening to release this file at a later date, however.

"It is done," a statement from CyberLeek reads. "[Cyberleek] holds the full November 2026 build of Grand Theft Auto 6, and it is going out by torrent. Now. Every file except one. The main executable is held on a countdown." CyberLeek says the executable will be released earlier than planned if its crypto token reaches a predetermined value. Many of the leaks to date have been related to a CyberLeek crypto scheme. Previously, it was estimated that the group cashed out at least £200,000.

What does all this mean? There's a very realistic chance that the game could be up and running on PC soon - undercutting Rockstar's unannounced PC release by a matter of months, if current rumours are to be believed. "This community will have it emulated inside a week, running far past 30fps," the statement continues. "[CyberLeek] told you not to preorder for a reason. This is one of the reasons.

"If the Xbox build cannot be made to work and support holds, [CyberLeek] will work to get a PS5 build - a fallback, most likely never required. Either way: the Xbox build is going out. No double dipping for Take-Two/Rockstar." It seems these are not empty threats.

CyberLeek has been a thorn in Rockstar's side for a while now. The group initially claimed it took this action in the name of "Gamers' Rights", supposedly fighting for consumers in relation to the controversial discontinuation of game-discs and the digital-only future being pursued by game publishers. Rockstar has previously issued statements regarding the leaker, noting that the leaks are "heartbreaking" and that "this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time". Take-Two tried to subpoena Discord for information pertaining to the leaker's identity.

#3787. Ubisoft says Assassin's Creed Jade is still alive as it merges two of its Creative Houses

Ubisoft has confirmed that while Assassin's Creed Jade - its mobile entry in the series - is still in development, its focus remains with console and PC.

Speaking during the earnings call for Ubisoft's first-half results, CFO Frédérick Duguet said mobile was "still an opportunity for the medium to longer term, with games such as AC Jade on Assassin’s Creed", according to a transcript of the call published by Investing.com.

"Looking at what we can see in terms of long-term financial return, in the mindset of having a stronger focus in terms of capital allocation and financial returns, we consider that we would rather put our resources on bigger opportunities," Duguet said. "Today, we can say that console and PC remain our core focus for our biggest franchises."

He added: "The focus is really to make sure that we come with strong growth on console and PC, and notably PC, which is a more dynamic platform than ever."

Ubisoft last confirmed its China-set mobile game was still in the works in March, when it was mentioned in the publisher’s Assassin's Creed: Into 2026 blog. Assassin's Creed now sits within Vantage Studios, Ubisoft's joint venture with Tencent, which launched last year.

Ubisoft's results also confirmed some more changes to the way the company is run, with the publisher saying its new operating model is "now fully in place". Creative Houses 3 and 5 have been combined under the leadership of Julien Bares "to leverage synergies between Live experiences across platforms".

All leadership roles across the Creative Houses are now filled, too. An external general manager has been appointed for Creative House 4 and is set to join in January 2027, though Ubisoft hasn't yet confirmed who. That follows September's appointment of 2K and Amazon Games veteran Christoph Hartmann to lead Creative House 2, home to The Division, Ghost Recon, and Splinter Cell, which was renamed Massive Entertainment at the same time.

Outside the Creative Houses, Motherbrain, the team behind Ubisoft's generative AI experiment Teammates, is now a subsidiary in its own right. It's working on "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds". A separate unit has also been set up to look after brands that don't belong to any of the Creative Houses.

Ubisoft says the new structure is already paying off, pointing to the commercial success of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced and renewed momentum for Rainbow Six Siege, which it says ranked among the top 10 games across Xbox and PlayStation for monthly active users over the half.

That said, the publisher nonetheless posted a net loss of €254.5 million for the first half of the year, with net bookings down 16.5 percent to €644.7 million.

The news comes just hours after Ubisoft confirmed 166 job cuts at its Montréal and Québec City studios, the latest in a year of layoffs. They're part of the "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" that Ubisoft announced in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

Since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

On the weekend, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on a new Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

#3786. Eldritch Empathy is a Papers Please-esque roguelite about diagnosing cosmic horror creatures and trying not to lose your marbles as you do

Oh I do love an eldritch horror creature, I do, especially one that at first glance may only be slightly different from what I'm used to seeing. Eldritch Empathy, then, seems like a grand ole game to satisfy my wanton need to experience such things. It's a puzzle roguelite that isn't exactly a Papers Please-like but certainly feels reminiscent of one, where you have to "analyse corrupted creatures, purify their emotions and learn how to communicate with an eldritch being."

You kick things off by embodying Eike, a "young woman who has strange dreams and sightings of twisted creatures in the woodlands neighbouring the sleepy Swiss village she lives in." She decides to investigate these mysterious circumstances herself, where she comes upon these corrupted critters in the woods. You need to thoroughly inspect them, using a book to determine what is going on with them and what they need exactly; it's akin to checking the passport rulebook in Papers Please, hence the comparison.

After figuring out what's going on with these creatures, you then "use and transform symbols to create paths through the creatures' insides. You may use care and precision to navigate to the correct corrupted emotion you have identified from your investigation and purify it. You may also use your tools to cause harm. Whatever you choose, your actions will have consequences." Ominous! You can also plan your runs ahead of time, heading down paths that may offer you some boons here and there, like the option to restore a bit of sanity (it's one of those Lovecraftian kind of horror games, as loathe as I am that we still have to reference that guy).

Also be wary of the fact that actions you take out in the woods can affect your home and community. It's a roguelite with consequences! Mwahahha! Looks pretty neat overall, and has some tasty pixel art attached to it too. No release date just yet, but I'd assume it'll arrive no earlier than next year. You can wishlist it right here.

My daily GTA 6 routines turned Jason into a birdwatcher and then a barely effective ecoterrorist

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

My Jason gets up at 7am every morning in GTA 6 and sips a cup of coffee while chatting with Lucia. Then he eats an apple, wanders onto the deck to work out, and comes back inside for a quick shower before plotting out his day. You've gotta be realistic, of course. There's no way he can make time to dive for Kenton's treasures and take on that next job with Donnie in an afternoon. But maybe there's time to swing by that fishing spot Cal mentioned and still get home in time to enjoy a few more scenes of domestic bliss.

I spent my first 20 or so hours playing GTA 6 like it was Stardew Valley rather than an action-packed crime epic, but that's OK by me, as I love the rhythm taking each new in-game day as its own little challenge. One night, scrolling social media while cuddled up with Lucia, I ran across a pilot looking for help up north, miles outside of Vice City. It'd be an all-day trip getting up there, but Jason had just gotten into meditation, and Lucia had mentioned a spot out on the edge of the swamp where he might be able to clear his head. Two birds with one stone.

After the usual morning routine, I hopped in the car and headed north, first toward that meditation spot. Surrounded by wildlife, this is the point where I realized you could use the binoculars to look around and study animals to add to the in-game compendium, and I spent more time than I care to admit simply enjoying the sights of the swamp and birdwatching. Oh, a great blue heron? Absolutely majestic.

I almost had time left to make it up to that pilot job, but I got distracted by an abandoned dinosaur-themed minigolf course on the roadside. I spent hours trying to perfect each hole. By the time I realized how late it had gotten, the sun was already getting low. The twilight put one thought in my mind: "Shit, I'd better get home so I can hang out with Lucia before she goes to sleep."

But my Jason, clearly awakened to the power of nature by his birdwatching experience, ended up having greater duties than that of a wife guy. Along one of the winding roads that led back home, I heard such a commotion that I had to investigate – a prize pageant cow named Tootsie had escaped from her owner's trailer and was making a break for it.

I headed her off with my car and got out to calmly talk her down, but as she finally settled I heard the words "save me" echoing in Jason's mind. Leading her back to the trailer, the owner is very grateful – even as he warns that Tootsie is destined for the slaughterhouse after her final run of shows. At this point, I realized who Jason was becoming. I let Tootsie run free, and when her owner got mad about it, I punched him in the face and stole his cowboy hat as he ran to his truck and drove away.

That alone might be enough to turn Jason into a hero of the animal rights movement, but the day was not yet done. As darkness settled in on the journey home, I was cruising along the highway on the outskirts of Vice City when I ran into a traffic jam. At first, I assumed this was just the last vestiges of rush hour traffic – but no, a group of activists was holding up an animal services truck which, they claimed, housed a wrongfully imprisoned bear.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Again, I knew what I had to do. I hopped out of my car, headed to the back door of the truck, and started punching it. (Look, I know I probably could've shot the lock off, but I wasn't about to fire a pistol on a busy highway and attract police attention.) As the traffic continued backing up for miles, the driver eventually panicked and hit the gas, running over one of the protesters in the process. As they screamed out for their fallen friend, I figured I better hop back in the car and drive off before things got any more heated.

Tragically, Lucia was already asleep by the time I got home, so I never got to see what Jason might've said about the day's ridiculous events. I did, however, get a little treat while scrolling Snapmatic in bed – an image of Tootsie looking so happy at the height of her pageant days. I hope, somewhere out in the wild, that she's living her best life.

#3783. Blizzard wants to "get rid" of best-in-slot items in World of Warcraft: Forever by introducing situationally strong gear

"BIS is not a good thing for a game that's supposed to be about role-playing."

With World of Warcraft: Forever's first raids set to release in early December, developers of the game have spoken about endgame itemisation and their desire to disrupt the "best-in-slot" (BIS) mindset that's been at the core of WoW's progression for years.

This information stems from the latest episode of the official World of Warcraft: Forever podcast. In it, senior game designer Aidan Moon revealed his philosophy around the game's itemisation, which he played - and plays - a major role in designing.

"I essentially want to get rid of BIS," Moon said. "I think BIS is not a good thing for a video game that's supposed to be about role-playing. That's why I've introduced the creature subtype system, where things are more effective against murlocs [for example]. We've introduced the biome system too, and in the raid it's different."

He gave an example from upcoming raid Barrow Deeps, which will be split into different biomes that offer opportunities for such creature subtype gear to be put to use. "If you go to the left wing that's snowy; if you go to the right wing, that's haunted; if you go down below, that's cavernous. ... I think your BIS should be different for every single boss if you're making a theoretical BIS list."

Moon acknowledged that the system is open for players to interact with to the extent they're comfortable with. Some players might bring optimised gear for certain bosses, while others might not, opting instead for generally good gear to perform well regardless of the fight.

It's an excitingly different approach that goes against the established norms of WoW's endgame raiding. In other versions in World of Warcraft, gear progression is more linear: people go into raids with an idea of what gear drops are best for their character, and intentionally hunt these pieces to replace the set they're wearing. It's a vertical sense of progression. Will theoretically having multiple sets of equipment, for multiple situations, change this?

Best-in-slot gear is an especially pertinent topic in WoW Forever at the moment, given the most dedicated players are reaching max level, or nearing it, and are hunting for items in preparation for the upcoming raid. I'm currently ticking off equipment from a best-in-slot list for a Balance Druid. Whether this player behavior will change when the changes are implemented remains to be seen. Perhaps the approach will expand, with players continuing to hunt down generally accepted 'good' items while also seeking side pieces that provide situational bonuses along the way.

The Blizzard discussion on raid itemisation went beyond standard power items. Chase items, those with especially low drop rates, were also talked about by Moon, noting that Barrow Deeps continues several such items that he hopes will keep players returning to it for years to come.

The items Moon is likely referring to here probably relate to mounts, pets, situational gear, and perhaps campfire bonuses.

For example, I obtained an upgraded campfire earlier in the game that allows a greater campfire to be built that allows more buff items to be placed around it.This has essentially locked me in as a campfire slave for the upcoming raid tier, and valuable to a raid composition.

World of Warcraft: Forever has proven extremely popular since its early November release. The game broke franchise records for Blizzard on launch, and has more weekly players than WoW has seen in 15 years. Judging from early impressions of World of Warcraft: Forever, the game has real merit.

#3782. Public-access television is born anew in NIGHT EYE TV, a digital goggle box filled with art game curios

I am both a bit too young and a bit too very not American to have ever experienced public-access television, but it's something that's always fascinated me. For those too young to have even heard of it, or just not in the know, it essentially allowed anyone to broadcast their own shows through cable TV. A proto YouTube, if you will. It's obviously not what it was any more, given the advent of the internet, but in NIGHTEYE.TV, it may be making a digital, more interactive return.

NIGHTEYE.TV is a strange little place. I call it a place, it's a fake TV floating in a Unity default texture void, lending it a Backroomsian vibe, but even if there's not much there to ground yourself in, the goggle box is enticing all the same. It beckons you to turn it on, a series of buttons all linking to different "channels." What awaits you isn't television, however. Instead you'll find games, mostly of the weirdo, freako, sicko variety, quickly setting the tone.

🌕NIGHT EYE TV’s initial form is live!🌑 Check out the site and follow our Indiegogo campaign at www.nighteye.tv![image or embed]

In its current incarnation, it's mostly just a collection of clips of these various art games, with direct links to them hidden away in a menu, but a good collection it is. You'll find Nathalie Lawhead's Everything is Going to Be OK, Jeremy Couillard's more recent Soul Injector Commando, and Taylor McCue's He Fucked The Girl Out Of Me. Some clips are longer than others, acting as sort of segments of playthroughs, but it all feels like an exciting evolution of what public-access television was.

The ultimate goal is for it to be a curated platform where you can buy a rotating selection of games. Most of the sale goes back to the original artist, and 15% gets put into a community pool to be split amongst all of the contributors, with the last 15% going towards keeping everything running. As it stands, that's not quite ready yet. You can help make it happen, though, as right now an Indiegogo campaign is running to help it all get fully operational. Worth chucking a few quid I reckon!

Grand Theft Auto 6 hasn't even been out for a week yet, and someone has already done the math on how many buildings in the whole of Leonida you can actually walk into. For those of you who are curious: it's 1,563 buildings.

That is frankly ridiculous. I don't think I've ever been inside 1,563 different buildings in my entire life, although I am a creature of habit, so that could explain things. The player who shared these stats, Aileos, does note that there are 5,588 buildings in total, so the enterable buildings only account for a fraction of that, just over 25%.

There are some who will look at this with a glass-half-empty perspective, and I get it. This world is so cool, it's easy to want more of it, but as another player points out, "This would've sent us into psychosis a few years back". Sometimes it's better to focus on what we have rather than what we don't have. After all, how many buildings will you realistically enter in your GTA 6 playthrough? Probably not 1,563.

We've spent the past week here in the PC Gamer Slack channel marvelling at just how many random encounters you can stumble across in GTA 6. Some of us have found sentient NPCs. One of us was actually recognised by a convenience store clerk who then asked to get robbed, and I think we've all seen videos of the furry rescue mission.

But just because this world already has loads of awesome activities, it doesn't mean we aren't hoping for more. A massive casino and go-kart track have been spotted by players, both of which have huge "Coming Soon" signs draped outside of them.

These buildings could be lying in wait for GTA 6 Online, or they could be added to singleplayer sometime in the future. Regardless, those are two more buildings that will potentially welcome players soon.

#3777. Alt Video is a digital, faux Blockbuster video store that you can fill with movies from your Letterboxd watchlist and Plex server

And you can even watch those movies in-game

Since the beginning of the year, I have watched almost 150 films. I know this, because over the past few years, I've become one of those people… a Letterboxd user. Gasp! I know, I know, but I don't think I'm too insufferable about it. I'll only do a joke review in the hopes of like farming if I think it's genuinely funny! But many of these films were watched digitally, meaning I don't have a bunch of DVDs to admire on a shelf. So what am I to do? Well, I could check out Alt Video, a not quite job simulator where you can use your Letterboxd account or media server to fill up a digital, faux Blockbuster.

This is, obviously, not so dissimilar to Boxroom, a game where you can design your own bedroom that lets you use your Steam profile to fill it with games you actually own. With Alt Video, you do things slightly differently just because of the focus on a different format. So, say you have a Letterboxd account. After exporting some data from your account, you can bring that into Alt Video, and this fake video store will then get filled up with shelves of DVD cases of all the films you've watched.

Alternatively, and perhaps more enticingly, if you run something like a Plex or Jellyfin server, you can hook that up to the game too, where again all of the films you own digitally show up in store. What's more interesting here is that there's a cinema room in the store that lets you watch films on your Plex server, and it's possible to invite your Steam friends to watch along with you. There's even a few other rooms, like a '90s bedroom or family room for more of a CRT kinda vibe. It's cute! If you like you can even manually add any DVDs or Blu-rays you own to appear on all the shelves too.

There's a lot of other nice touches too. In the case of your Letterboxd data, your ratings even show up on the back of the boxes. It's not just relegated to films either, you can put in shows or even your games. The whole thing can be played in VR if you really want that immersive feel. There's a store clerk who can give you some recommendations if you're not sure what to watch. And there's even a day and night system, weather, and seasonal shopfront facelifts.

Alt Video is currently slated for release next week on November 24th, and it'll be doing so in early access. Worth noting that for now the focus is on the browsing, but features involving serving customers and running the store are on the way. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#3775. GTA 6 day-one sales are enormous, estimates suggest, making previous $2 billion opening weekend predictions seem conservative

Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have sold nearly 25 million copies in one day, generating approximately $2.5bn in sales revenue - a staggering result that's beyond even what even observers were predicting.

The estimates come from data-tracking company Sensor Tower (spotted by VGC), which has been watching GTA 6 pre-orders closely for weeks, updating estimates daily based on (unspecified) data that it collects.

Should the results be accurate, it'll dramatically eclipse GTA 6's $1bn in three days result. It'll also put GTA 6 on track to reach the eye-watering $3.25bn to $5.2bn week-one sales estimates for GTA 6.

So far, Rockstar has said nothing in relation to GTA 6's sales since the game was released around the world yesterday. Parent company Take-Two has said the game's pre-orders were tracking "well above expectations, and GTA 6 broke pre-order records on both the PlayStation Store and the Xbox Store, though, so all signs point to a record-breaking release. The question is "by how much?".

Reaction to GTA 6 has been glittering. Chris awarded GTA 6 five golden stars in Eurogamer's review, calling it "a game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale". "Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that."

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for googling local purveyors of live Christmas trees, the sole upside of no longer having a cat being that you can once again enjoy the smell of chopped woodland without the risk of it poisoning a family member. Finally, five words: Neil the Seal Management Plan.

The accents will be from all over Britain as well

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Go big or go home. Playground Games is pushing to make Fable 4 the largest installment of the RPG series to date, at least in terms of the amount of dialog. According to the devs, there are tens of thousands of lines of dialogue, recorded in accents spanning the length and breadth of the British Isles.

Ralph Fulton, the general manager of Fable and co-founder of Playground Games, explains what's gone into the voice-acting with GamesIndustry.biz. "Over a hundred voice actors from all over the UK have contributed to the game, recording over 150,000 lines of dialogue," he says. "It's a mammoth operation."

That's a hefty cast, and a considerable amount of scripting. For comparison, Skyrim has around 60,000 lines of spoken dialogue, and Mass Effect contains around 40,000. Those are big RPGs, with a lot of characters to meet and chat to.

Fallout 4 is closer, sitting at 111,000 or so. Hitting six figures is a truly monumental amount of work, and it's taken Playground over 1,000 hours of work this year alone, across multiple studios, to get through everyone's lines.

In tandem with this, the team's been making sure you can hear a variety of backgrounds on your journey through the grand adventure. "We were really keen to make sure that there are accents from every corner of the UK, not just your standard fantasy RP accents, but someone from Sheffield, someone from Belfast, someone from Edinburgh," Fulton explains.

"And that brings a certain amount of humor to it naturally," he continues, "because with regional accents, you have funny ways of expressing things, and I think that just adds to the Britishness of the game."

I'd agree, though I may need subtitles for certain dialects. But that's all part of the charm, really.

#3771. Total War: Warhammer 40,000 breaks the game into star system mini-campaigns, each with their own stories and objectives

"We want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy."

There is perhaps nothing so brutal in a Total War game than getting an army full of elite units wiped out, and it appears that pain remains a factor in the upcoming Total War conversion of : Warhammer 40,000. Creative Assembly also has some nifty ideas around breaking the game into mini-campaigns for each star system you visit.

In an hour-long deep-dive livestream of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, developer Creative Assembly demonstrated the game in action, focusing initially on how armies navigate from planet to planet. Each star system apparently acts as a "contained campaign" you can hop between in the game.

The star system the stream focused on is Praevoss, a mid-sized collection of planets: three of which you can land on and fight on, while the others are smaller and unable to support your tactical warfare shenanigans. Once you're finished with a star system, you move on, carrying over units and unlocked skills.

"First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," Creative Assembly explained on the livestream. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start, [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do."

One of the objectives highlighted in the livestream was an Ork Scourge, which required the player - controlling Space Marines - to hold the planet while eradicating the Ork presence.

As you can imagine, much of the stream was dedicated to the fleet of spaceships at your disposal - fleet movement and management, and the abilities they provide to your armies such as orbital bombardments. There was also detail on how ships transport troops, as well as the upgrades you can build to further enhance their power.

On the topic of transporting troops, the developers focused on the small number of expensive but powerful Space Marines they controlled. These Space Marine armies come with a potentially "devastating" cost if you mess up and lose your armies during one of the star system campaigns.

"Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the developers explained. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that."

Total War: Warhammer 40,000 is set to release some time in 2027, though no specific date has been established as of writing. Much has been seen at this point on its gameplay, galactic or otherwise. As we near the end of the year, fans are clamouring for official word on when they can take to the stars.

After eight years of operation, the Atari Homebrew Awards are no more.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Atari Homebrew Awards, an annual celebration of new games developed for old systems by the people who love them both, has been cancelled after eight years of operation—and yes, it's because of AI.

"As you may know, the landscape of retro game development changed dramatically this year with the massively increased capabilities of LLMs. More and more games have incorporated AI elements into their development chain and now have the capability to create full games without writing a single line of code," Atari Homebrew Awards host James, aka ZeroPage Homebrew, wrote on the Atari Age forums.

"Keeping up with the large number of AI-assisted game development had become increasingly difficult as this year wore on, with some developers even releasing multiple games a week with the aid of AI. This flood of new AI games forced me to re-evaluate the way games were qualified and judged for the upcoming AHAs.

"The Atari Homebrew Awards were now challenged to make sure the work of human developers were still honoured amongst the new fully computer-coded games. I was not at all interested in giving awards to the output of large language models, only to humans who coded their own games, but I quickly discovered that this was going to be more difficult than I thought."

James said he discovered last week that "a large majority" of developers were using AI in some capacity to make their games, from testing to wholesale game creation, "without one typed line of code."

That left two options: Disallow any and all AI usage in the Atari Homebrew Awards competition, which James said would disqualify a large number of "extremely talented coders" who used AI in some very minor way, or let it slide and either choose an arbitrary dividing line between what is and isn't allowed or allow everything, including fully vibe-coded games.

James said he wasn't interested in that, which meant he needed to settle on how much AI usage would be allowable—and also how to determine if AI was used at all, since some developers are better at disclosure than others. That, naturally, led to the worry that developers could be subject to "false positives and possible witch hunts," something that's already a problem in mainstream game development.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

This is an extremely upsetting conclusion for this event because honouring all the hard work the community put into these games is always a highlight of my year.

Ultimately, James decided there was no practical way forward, although he did leave open the possibility of a return someday. "This is an extremely upsetting conclusion for this event because honouring all the hard work the community put into these games is always a highlight of my year," he wrote. "I know many others feel the same way and I hope to be able to continue this tradition in the coming years as things settle into a new normal."

As we noted in July, debates over "acceptable" levels of AI use are cropping up all over the open source development scene: Some are drawing hard lines against it for principled and/or practical reasons, yet its popularity is growing explosively because, frankly, you don't need to know what you're doing in order to do it—as long as you're not too concerned with doing it well.

The Atari Homebrew Awards isn't the first such event to fall victim to the AI flood. Earlier in November, the Australian STEM Videogame Challenge, a "free national videogame development competition for students," announced that the 2026 event will be its last because "the rapid and complex rise of generative AI in game development [made] it harder to judge what students made themselves," and thus undercut the whole purpose of the program: Encouraging kids to learn how to code.

From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

#3767. Undisclosed AI-generated music pulled from The Binding of Isaac Repentance+ update, as attempt to get satirical on GTA 6 launch day goes awry

Original creator Edmund McMillen said he "had no idea [the update] featured generated music in the daily run"

An update for The Binding of Isaac packed with wink wink, nudge nudge parody of GTA 6 has backfired rather spectacularly, with publishers Nicalis having to make some hasty modifications. This free addition to the Repentance+ version of the roguelike featured a Grand Terry Auto-inspired daily run, complete with cops, guns, and a soundtrack players soon highlighted as sounding AI-generated. Sure enough, Nicalis subsequently announced the "removal of generated music files" in response to the backlash.

The Repentance+ update went live on November 19th to coincide with GTA 6's release, and the music files had been yanked by Nicalis as of November 21st. In the interim, a Reddit user with the handle ShweetsStuff unearthed metadata pointing to AI tune generator Suno attached to some of the update's music files. Cue understandable questioning of why the DLC's Steam page hadn't had a disclosure of this genAI use slapped across it.

Original Binding of Isaac creator Edmund McMillen seems to have quickly ended up with inboxes full of folks asking him about what'd happened and demanding action. "Woke up to a shit show," he posted on the former Twitterverse on the 21st. Obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned."

Given the new build yanking the music went live later that day, McMillen's voice maybe only added to the chorus of complaints Nicalis were already aware of and facing. Either way, the songs are gone and Nicalis don't look to have said anything as of writing about whether they'll be replaced at some point down the line.

This isn't the first time a developer has considered using AI to generate songs designed to satirise or parody. In the case of Future? No Thanks! dev Paolo 'Molleindustria' Pedercini, the aim was partly to poke fun at disclosures, with people in the game's future society listening to AI-generated tunes that're corporately mandated to mention AI in the lyrics. Pedercini ended up deciding not to use AI-generated music in the final release.

On the face of it, while the effectiveness of using AI-generated songs to parody AI-generated songs is questionable, the argument for it seems stronger in a more focused satire like Future? No Thanks! than in the case of The Binding of Isaac having a GTA 6-related giggle. I've not listened to the Repentance+ update's AI tunes, but there's nothing obvious to indicate that their satirical job wouldn't have been done as well or better by Nicalis commissioning or otherwise employing someone to pen some entirely human-made ditties, that spoofed the nature of Large Stealy Wheely.

Perhaps the publishers will now go and do just that.

#3766. UK Prime Minister won't be playing GTA 6, government says, while hailing Rockstar Games a "British success story"

Grand Theft Auto 6's seismic launch has registered on a governmental level. A spokesperson for UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has hailed the game as a "British success story", but confirmed Burnham himself won't be playing it. His diary is apparently "very full".

"Rockstar Games is a British success story made in Edinburgh," a Downing Street spokesperson told The Independent - referencing the series' Scottish origins and ongoing development at Rockstar North - "and many fans are already saying GTA has been worth the wait." When asked if Burnham will be making time for GTA 6, the spokesperson responded: "His diary is very full. He won't be playing it."

Downing Street went on to address the issue of teenagers potentially skipping school to play the game, emphasising that children "should be in classrooms" this week because "every day in school matters".

The leader of Labour's opposition, the Conservative party's Kemi Badendoch, recently expressed similar concerns. "I know people are worried about the game content," she wrote. "At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half-an-hour on it and then went out and did something else."

GTA 6's culture-shaking success was unlikely to pass without reference by the government, but the celebratory tone is a marked departure from Burnham's predecessor Kier Starmer calling Rockstar's firing of 34 staff last year "deeply concerning". We are awaiting a verdict in the resulting employment tribunal related to it.

This state recognition of GTA 6 is not without precedent. It wasn't long ago that French President Emmanuel Macron congratulated Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on its award-winning and heart-winning success. That game sold 8 million copies in one year; GTA 6 is estimated to have sold 25 million copies in one day.

GTA 6 has been hailed as a generational release - an exorbitantly luxurious game that "pushes back the horizon of video games", Chris Tapsell wrote in Eurogamer's GTA 6 review.

#3764. Nvidia release hotfix for latest graphics card driver battering SSDs with excessive writes, but it looks like reverting may still be the better option

621.35 appears not to completely atone for 621.24's sins

Late last week, reports emerged of some folks having Nvidia's latest GeForce driver, 621.24, needlessly write vast amounts of data to their PC's SSD, a bug that could affect the component's lifespan at a time when replacing SSDs certainly isn't cheap. The immediate short-term solution for affected users was to roll back to a previous driver, 621.01. Sadly it appears that might still be the best way to go despite Nvidia having released a hotfix.

The hotfix, driver version 621.35, was released on November 20th and as of writing is only available to download directly from the Nvidia website. It's designed to address one issue, this being that "excessive writes to file nvlog.nvlgstg may occur in background".

"Since we have so many changes being checked in, we usually try to align driver releases with significant game or product releases," Nvidia wrote in their announcement of the hotfix. "This process has served us pretty well over the years but it has one significant weakness. Sometimes a change that is important to many users might end up sitting and waiting until we are able to release the driver. The fixes that make it in are based in part on your feedback in the Driver Feedback threads and partly on how realistic it is for us to quickly address them. These fixes (and many more) will be incorporated into the next official driver release, at which time the hotfix driver will be taken down.

"To be sure, these Hotfix drivers are beta, optional and provided as-is. They are run through a much abbreviated QA process. The sole reason they exist is to get fixes out to you more quickly. The safest option is to wait for the next WHQL certified driver. But we know that many of you are willing to try these out."

Unfortunately, it seems that based on some testing by users on r/Nvidia, the hotfix makes the situation with excessive SSD writing less bad than it is with 621.24, but doesn't eliminate the problem entirely. According to one of these users, 621.35 stops the excessive writing from starting right after you boot up and reduces the amount that's being written when the issue's at its peak, but doesn't prevent some excessive writing creeping in if hardware is left running for extended periods or left idling overnight.

Given that, rolling back to 621.01 still appears to be the most effective way of keeping the writes at an acceptable level while waiting for Nvidia to release a new driver than can permanently do away with the problem. One would hope it won't take too long, especially given the 621.24 driver still doesn't look to have been pulled offline so no one else grabs it prior to a fix arriving.

If you want to check if you're suffering from the excessive writing you'll need to open task manager, head to the 'details' tab, right click on the column header, click 'select columns', select 'I/O write bytes' from the menu of check boxes that brings up, then look for 'NVDisplay.Container.exe'. The number next that exe is in bytes, so you'll need to do some maths to work out if it's only writing a matter of MB or chunks of GB.

#3763. Star Wars: Galactic Racer studio "didn't dream" Biddy Blas would be as popular as he is

"He's always known exactly who he is, and he wears it proudly."

Fuse Games, the developer of Star Wars: Galactic Racer, has said it "didn't dream" the pod racing game's background character Biddy Blas would become as popular as he has.

Since Galactic Racer's release in October, Blas - who resembles a short, humanoid crocodile (officially a crocin) - has become a viral sensation. The combination of his unexpected swagger and ridiculous high-pitched Huttese monologues - performed irresistibly by actor Richard Summers-Calvert - have made him a fan favourite, especially his catchphrase "scrib doon" (which means "write it down").

"Here's a name for you, amateur!" Blas tells the player upon meeting them, albeit in Huttese. "Biddy Blas. Write it down. Tattoo it on your arm, and someday your arm will be worth millions!"

Fuse Games shared a comment from Biddy Blas creator and Galactic Racer narrative designer Ren Alex-Rose about the character's success. "We always suspected Biddy Blas would be a popular member of the Galactic League, but we didn't dream of just how popular he'd become," Alex-Rose said.

"He was an incredibly enjoyable character to build, from our early ideation of a small, angry non-human character (who we lovingly referred to as our cast's 'chaos goblin') to recording his sometimes-absurdist dialogue with Blas' voice actor, who took the crocin to a whole new level.

"It's been great watching Biddy Blas emerge into his assured self, as well as seeing the community embrace him for it. He's always known exactly who he is, and he wears it proudly."

Blas' breakout success was praised by Lucasfilm producer Craig Derrick, who said his social feeds were filled with posts about Galactic Racer, though mostly about Biddy Blas. And the enthusiasm actor Richard Summers-Calvert was greeted with during October's MCM Comic-Con in London, which I attended, was palpable. There's a nice video of him doing Blas' voice on Instagram.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer was awarded a full five stars in Eurogamer's review. "Both a surprisingly fun Roguelite campaign and a racing treat for Criterion fans, this is just wonderful stuff," wrote Christian Donlan.

From two-month plans to an annual subscription

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there's any kind of Black Friday deal I reliably hunt for, its discounts on streaming service subscriptions. These aren't too expensive, but over many months it can add up, and so a discounted entry point can pay off loads in the long run. I always take to the holiday discounts to get my next subscription, and I've already found mine for 2027.

In total, nine different streaming platforms are offering Black Friday deals — two of them are via a bundle, so in effect there are eight discounts, but some have multiple options . These range from massive discounts on shorter packages, which we'll start with, to a few six-month options, and then several which will last you a full year. Just remember, the best discount isn't necessarily on the cheapest streaming service subscription, but on whichever you've already been thinking about checking out.

Fubo is offering you $30 off your first month of a subscription (after the free trial), with the cheapest eligible plan being the Sports + News one. The discount applies to more expensive tiers though, with the same flat rate reduction.

Peacock has a range of discounts, including the Select plan being at $2.99 for three months (but skip this; Select is too limited) but the best limited-term discount is this. For a three months, you can save $4 on your monthly bill. It's a nice price saving if you wanted Peacock anyway, but there's a better one...

If you want a year of Peacock, this is the best deal, as it'll cost you much less in the long run than the above deal. Premium and Select both have reductions on their annual plan, but the less said about Select the better.

Apple's premium TV streaming is half price for half a year, which is significant as it's not as prone to discounts as its rivals. Honestly, this is the deal I'm jumping on: it's enough time to enjoy a solid selection of shows, without being so long that I run out of stuff to watch. Apple's library sounds great too, especially with more Bad Monkey on the way.

Each of Crunchyroll's three tiers are greatly reduced, with the cheapest being Fan. This gets you access to the entirety of the service's anime library, just without some of the manga and games that the higher tiers offer. If you want more, the deals make the highest tier, Ultimate Fan, cheaper than standard Fan is outside of sales.

I imagine this'll be one of the most popular streaming deals: Disney Plus and Hulu are bundled together for just $5 per month for an entire year, if you're happy with the ad plan. Want ad-free streaming? That bundle is also reduced, down to $14.99 over the same span of time.

Almost as cheap as the Disney deal, this discount gets you access to another major streamer. Again, it's for an ad-supported tier, and the price is less than $1 more than Disney's cost (although it's just for one platform).

This is a massive discount, getting you access to a whole streaming service for just $12. Admittedly, Starz isn't as full of content as rivals, but it's still got the Power shows, Outlander and a few other pieces.

No matter the percentage or money reduction in the subscription cost of a streaming service, a deal's no good if you're not going to use the platform in question. For example, as someone who doesn't watch anime, a Crunchyroll discount isn't exactly a great deal for me.

So you should probably let your interests guide your hand when picking a deal. Want access to an existing library of movies? Disney Plus, Peacock and Paramount Plus are right there. Prefer to watch some prestige TV? You've got Apple TV and Starz. And if you've got a growing watch-list of shows, steer towards the platform they're on.

I like to pick one streaming service per year, and enjoy a year's discounts on it. Last year, I went with half price on the monthly cost of Now TV (the UK's precursor to HBO Max), and now I've tapped out most of the shows I wanted to watch. This year, it's Apple TV I want to catch up on. Rinse and repeat, and in a couple of years, each library will be repopulated with shows to watch.

It's also worth asking how long you want your subscription to last. If you just want to skim through a streamers' library and pick a few movies to watch, you don't need a 12-month. But if you think you'll stick around for the long term, these deals will be preferable, where some of the two-month discounts won't let you scratch the surface and could cost you more on the long run.

There's a lot more discounted: check out the Black Friday toy deals for lots of entertainment. Alternatively, we're collecting Black Friday retro deals worth knowing about.

#3759. Nightdive's Thief remaster will make the most "infamous" Thief Gold level a little less maddening, by "just kind of pointing the player in the right direction"

On bringing Thieves Guild up to snuff with the Haunted Cathedral and co

1999's Thief Gold is widely considered the definitive incarnation of Thief: The Dark Project, adding three levels to the Looking Glass stealth sim while tidying up some bugs, but it has one grievous failing, in the eyes of many: the notorious Thieves Guild. In this all-new sixth mission, master catburglar Garrett must infiltrate the lair of a gang of pickpockets, after they filch a vase he had his eye on. The lair in question is actually very believable, as a hideout for criminals, in that it resists exploration even with a paper map. It consists of sunken, samey, obtusely arranged rooms that are made all the more headache-inducing by objectives that require a lot of backtracking.

In much the same way that I can admire a finely wrought pair of thumbscrews, I think the Thieves Guild is a clever creation, one that arguably shines when you use every ability or tactic in Garrett's possession rather than trying to ghost it. But it very easily becomes frustrating, to the point that many grizzled housebreakers advise new players to skip the level entirely. The Thieves Guild should be less frustrating in Nightdive's forthcoming Thief: The Dark Project Remastered, thanks to a more revealing spread of environmental textures and various other, furtive adjustments. As with many mods or remasters that speak of boosting the "immersion", I do worry that something valuable is being sacrificed in the process.

In the course of a wide-ranging interview about how they're reworking this most devious of Dark Projects, Nightdive producer Daniel Grayshon explained that the map changes are "more in terms of background tech", than altering the fundamental design or introducing details that oblige different strategies. "They've gone into these levels in a sensible way to fix some practical problems with them, like some issues where you might be able to climb up to a place that you shouldn't have been able to climb up before," he commented.

The Thief remaster team have taken more liberties, seemingly, with some of the Thief Gold maps. "Because some of the levels that were introduced in Thief Gold - they felt quite blocky and quite rushed, maybe, as you go through them," Grayshon explained. "But our team again, they've been able to go through and completely renovate some of these levels. The Opera House now feels in some parts like an actual Opera House, instead of a couple of blocky rooms. So I think players will really look at these and think, oh yeah, these kinds of details make sense, without it being too disruptive or too immersion breaking…"

"One particular - maybe people will consider infamous - level of the Gold package would be the Thieves Guild," Grayshon added. "The Thieves Guild is, if I were to sum it up kind of briefly, it is maybe two hours of walking through what feels like sewers, the same environment over and over again. There was no real visual distinction as to where you are in the level.

"So, we acknowledged pretty quickly that we need to go in and look at the Thieves Guild and fix it up, and what we've been able to do is texture it a lot more effectively. Give areas distinct looks, without compromising any of the gameplay again, like I mentioned. So we've put a bit more signposting around as well. Nothing that's going to be intrusive or immersion breaking again. Just kind of pointing the player in the right direction, as well as some other little things that I'm not going to spoil too much, but I think players will maybe appreciate the effort that we've done for this one."

In general, Nightdive's broad aim has been "bringing those Gold levels up to the quality of the original and then taking all of those levels and then bumping them up to the next level - almost Thief 2 levels of quality in its environment design, especially in some of the mansions, and some of the later levels," Grayshon said. "That's the level we were aiming for."

I have Several Thoughts about Grayshon's thoughts above (yes, people who dislike huffy armchair theory, this is your cue to skip to the comments). One is that I continue to dislike "immersion" as an ideal, though I recognise that many devs just use it as easy shorthand for a bunch of ways of doing art, sound and interface design. I think it often translates to uninvestigated enthusiasm for photorealistic fidelity and experiences that feel "smooth" and "engaging" enough to induce a kind of chemical trance. Many of the games I consider most valuable are cranky and unwilling and jarring, requiring you to think critically about the simulation rather than 'losing yourself' inside it. As regards the original Thief specifically, I enjoy how its nigh-magical stealth induces feelings of wavering dissociation, and keeps me guessing about the solidity of my own body.

Secondly, there's the age-old argument that if you're going to preserve a game faithfully, you should preserve what it did badly. The Thieves Guild is a legend among players, much as Blighttown is among Dark Souls players and the Library is among fans of Halo: Combat Evolved. You learn much about the methodology of Thief at large from the guild's stifling contours, and it's thrilling to witness a bunch of very smart designers take a swing at a concept and not quite connect. I'll try to hold onto that rousing sentiment, when I'm playing the remaster and struggling to remember where they hid that damn vase.

#3758. GTA 6 players are already pulling off high-flying tricks and other impressive stunts, just days after launch

One of the best things to emerge from Grand Theft Auto over the years has been the community's truly spectacular stunts: players soaring under bridges, leaping across buildings, and more. And with GTA 6's release this week, we've seen the first signs of the trend continuing in a brand-new world.

This TikTok video by user Gstitz from early in GTA 6, for instance, claims to be the "world's first" demonstration of a Mallard flying sideways between a narrow gap in a large building. It takes several attempts, but they eventually pull off the stunt without crashing or broken parts.

Another video from Hazardous is a more grounded (literally) look at Grand Theft Auto 6, and shows the YouTuber flinging motorbikes and cars around the map as they explore promising high-risk jumps. Some of these locations are tied to in-game challenges, so there are certainly breadcrumbs placed by Rockstar to encourage such ventures.

Granted, these are far from the truly absurd stunts we've seen in prior Grand Theft Auto games. But as a firing gun for the wider community, it's a great start. They're also among the most impressive things we've seen in GTA 6's opening week.

It's doubtless been an eventful few days though. Players have been entranced by the slapstick violence and in-game social media. Even UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has praised the game, despite not having time to actually play it. Eurogamer editor-in-chief Chris Tapsell also came away impressed, lauding it in his five star GTA 6 review.

The DOGE alum Treasury CIO says his passion project is "so cool."
